title: Rollators With a Seat and Brakes: How to Choose One for Everyday Walking
subtitle: A plain-English guide to wheeled walkers with a built-in seat, what to check before buying, and how to use the brakes safely.
excerpt: A rollator lets you walk farther and sit down when you need a break, but the seat is only safe when the brakes are locked. Here is what to check before you buy one.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: A walk to the mailbox, a trip down the grocery aisle, a stroll around the block. These are simple things until your legs tire halfway through and there is nowhere to sit. That is often the moment people start looking at a rollator.

A rollator is a walker on wheels with a seat built in. You push it ahead of you as you walk, and when you need a rest, you lock the brakes, turn around and sit down. For many people it means going farther, more often, with a place to rest along the way.

A rollator usually has a seat and two swiveling front wheels, according to Consumer Reports (in an article that is a couple of years old). The swiveling helps you steer around corners and through doorways. Hand brakes sit on the handles. Squeeze them to slow down, and lock them to hold the rollator still.
That locking step matters most. A seat is a fall risk if the brakes are not locked first, so make sure you can lock them easily and do it every time you sit.

A rollator is not right for everyone. It rolls on four wheels, so it may not suit someone who needs to lean on their walker for support. One seller's guidance says standard walkers are the safer choice in that case, and we could not confirm that with a second source, so please ask your doctor or a physical therapist which type of walker is right for you. A rollator also is not a fit if you cannot press or pull the brakes, or cannot lift a folded frame into a car.

items: Brakes you can work easily. Try squeezing and locking them yourself. Consumer Reports advises making sure the locking mechanism is easy to use, since you need it whenever you sit.
Weight capacity. Check the listed weight rating against the user's weight. Vive lists 300 lb for its Lightweight model.
A comfortable seat. Consumer Reports says to look for "a padded seat with back support and a basket."
Folding and lifting. If the rollator will ride in a car, make sure the person using it, or whoever drives, can fold it and lift it in.
Storage. A basket or bag helps carry a purse or groceries. Accessories such as bags and trays are often sold separately, so check what is included.
Warranty. Terms vary by brand and model. Read the product page for the warranty details before you order.

sections.content: Setting it up and using it well

Ask your doctor or physical therapist to help you adjust the rollator to fit you and to show you how to sit down and stand up with it safely. They can also tell you whether a rollator suits your balance and strength.

Practice at home before heading out. Walk a few laps around the living room, and get comfortable squeezing and locking the brakes. Lock them before every sit, and make sure the rollator is not going to move.
Every so often, check that the brakes still grip firmly and the wheels turn smoothly. If anything feels loose, contact the maker before using it again.

Make locking the brakes a habit before every sit, every time, even for a few seconds. If the person using the rollator cannot lock the brakes without effort, that model is not the right fit. Also confirm the weight rating and the product details on the maker's page before you order.
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: A good rollator can make daily walks feel easier and a little less worrying. Take your time choosing, try the brakes, and bring in a doctor or physical therapist if you are unsure. Then enjoy the walk, and the rest stops along the way.
